content:
Although Apple has tried to shield Jony Ive from its lawsuit against OpenAI, it may not be able to keep the former design chief out of the dispute. Here's why.

OpenAI has the opportunity to put Apple in an extremely awkward position

In the lawsuit accusing OpenAI of stealing trade secrets, Apple has deliberately avoided mentioning Jony Ive, even though the hardware company Ive founded, io Products, is working with OpenAI on the very hardware at the centre of Apple's allegations.

Apple at one point in the lawsuit claimed that "OpenAI and its associates have engaged in organised misconduct at an institutional level," which includes io, but described it only as "a startup co-founded by Mr. Tan and other former Apple executives." Apart from the two individuals directly accused of wrongdoing, Tang Tan and Chang Liu, the lawsuit makes no mention of Ive, Evans Hankey, or any other former Apple executives.

Although it is still too early to say whether Ive will be called to the witness stand, the possibility certainly exists, especially if OpenAI decides to deploy him to make Apple uncomfortable—or at least feel uneasy.

This would put Apple in a highly delicate situation. Since leaving in 2019, Ive has publicly maintained a posture of deep respect for the company; his public appearances and interviews are typically carefully orchestrated.

These include appearances at events with Laurene Powell Jobs and his ongoing involvement with the Steve Jobs Archive. Earlier this year, Ive even penned a letter as part of the Archive's "Letters to a Young Creator" project, sharing anecdotes about working with Jobs.

Apple, for its part, appears to be reciprocating the courtesy, carefully managing its distance from the controversial decisions made during Ive's final years, including the MacBook butterfly keyboard. The company's apparent desire to keep Ive at arm's length from this lawsuit is consistent with that approach.

But once the case enters the discovery phase, Apple does not have complete control over who gets pulled in. Given Ive's role in founding io Products and overseeing the hardware project in question, OpenAI could argue that he has relevant knowledge about the product development process, the materials the team relied on, and whether Apple's trade secrets were used.

Apple could then find itself in the awkward position of questioning Ive under oath, challenging his testimony, or attempting to undermine the credibility of the executive who shaped many of Apple's iconic products.

This is not the first time Ive has given evidence in litigation involving Apple. In 2012, he was deposed in Apple's patent lawsuit against Samsung, where he answered questions about Apple's design process and early iPhone and iPad prototypes.

However, testifying for the opposing side could damage the carefully maintained relationship he has with Apple, and could even create friction with OpenAI—if Ive feels the company has dragged him into the fray unnecessarily just to pressure his former employer.

Do you think Jony Ive will be drawn into this lawsuit? Let us know your thoughts in the comments.
